title: Twelve Beds at 29th and Dearborn: Provident Hospital Opens
dek: Asked in 1890 to get one Black woman into a Chicago nursing school, Daniel Hale Williams helped start a hospital and training school of their own.

story.company: Provident Hospital and Training School Association
story.event: Founding an interracial hospital and nurses' school in a twelve-bed house in Chicago
story.summary: After Emma Reynolds was refused by every Chicago nursing school because she was Black, her brother, the Reverend Louis Reynolds, asked the surgeon Daniel Hale Williams for help. Williams and community leaders instead raised money for a hospital and training school open to all races, which opened with twelve beds at 29th and Dearborn Streets on 4 May 1891. Its first nurses, Reynolds among them, graduated in October 1892, and in 1898 it moved to a 65-bed building.
paragraphs: One evening in December 1890, by his biographer's account, Dr Daniel Hale Williams went to the parsonage of the Reverend Louis Reynolds of St Stephen's African Methodist Episcopal Church on Chicago's West Side. Reynolds's sister Emma wanted to train as a nurse. Every nursing school in the city had turned her down because she was Black, and her brother hoped Williams, a well-connected surgeon, could get her in.

Williams knew the problem was bigger than one place on one course. He had qualified at Chicago Medical College in 1883, but like the city's few other Black doctors he had little or no access to hospital wards, and he operated in patients' homes. Rather than lobby for a single student, he and a group of Black ministers, doctors and businessmen set out to found a hospital with its own nursing school, open to patients of every race and staffed by Black and white doctors together. Rallies were held on the South and West Sides. Not everyone agreed: at one meeting, Helen Buckler records, the lawyer John G. Jones objected that it would be a segregated hospital, and then doubted Black Chicagoans could keep one running. Williams replied, by her account, that "a people who don't make provision for their own sick and suffering are not worthy of civilization."

They began small on purpose. A commitment from the Armour meatpacking company helped with the down payment on a three-storey brick house at 29th and Dearborn Streets with room for twelve beds, and Williams argued they should not attempt more at first. The charter promised free treatment for the sick poor; the first year's budget came to $5,429. Neighbours gave a stove, a wringer, sheets and leftover vegetables. Provident Hospital opened on 4 May 1891. Williams insisted that nurses' training be "most rigid" and last eighteen months. In the first year 175 women applied, ten were accepted and seven enrolled.

On 27 October 1892 four nurses graduated, Emma Reynolds among them; in 1895 she qualified as a doctor. Austin Curtis, the first physician to train in surgery under Williams, later became surgeon-in-chief at Freedmen's Hospital in Washington. Twelve beds were soon not enough, and in 1898 Provident moved to a new building at 36th and Dearborn with 65.

quote.text: swathe not thine heart in thine hoard, for thou art become the steward of the endowments of the God. Thou art not the last; another shall be thine equal
quote.work: The Instruction of Ptahhotep (and of Ke'gemni)
quote.source_title: The Instruction of Ptah-Hotep and the Instruction of Ke'Gemni, tr. Battiscombe G. Gunn, Project Gutenberg eBook #30508
quote.connection: Ptahhotep tells the person who has risen to hold what they have gained as a trust, because others will come after and equal them. Williams, shut out of hospital wards himself, spent his standing on a place where the next nurses and doctors could be trained.

reflection: Williams was asked for a favour: a word in the right ear to get one woman onto one course. He could have made it and gone home. Instead he looked at why the favour was needed and built something so that the next woman would not have to ask.

Not every request deserves that answer; most days the favour is enough, and you have limited evenings. But when the same problem keeps arriving at your door in different faces, it may be asking for a small, durable fix rather than another kindness. Twelve beds was a modest start, chosen deliberately.
invitation: Think of a request you have answered more than twice this year, at work or at home. Write one sentence describing the smallest lasting change that would mean nobody has to ask you again.

research_notes: Dates: the Provident Foundation and Cook County Health date Emma Reynolds's refusals to 1889 and Williams's consultations to 1890; Buckler dates the evening at the Reynolds parsonage to December 1890. The story uses Buckler's December 1890 for the meeting, attributed to her. The association was incorporated in January 1891 (Buckler gives 23 January); Mapping Care and Buckler give 4 May 1891 as the opening, which the story uses. First graduates: Mapping Care, citing the Chicago Tribune of 28 October 1892, gives a first graduation on 27 October 1892 of four nurses including Emma Reynolds; the International Museum of Surgical Science says Reynolds and three classmates were the first graduates in 1894. The story uses the Tribune-sourced date. Mapping Care says Reynolds graduated from the Women's Medical College of Chicago in 1895; Buckler says only that she became an MD. Money: the Provident Foundation gives a first annual budget of $5,429; Buckler says early appeals raised $2,114.03 and the first year would need about twice that, and that P. D. Armour personally gave $200, whereas the Foundation and Hektoen credit the Armour company with the house's down payment. The story uses the Foundation's budget and says only that a commitment from Armour helped with the down payment. Buckler's 1954 biography is written in a novelistic style with reconstructed dialogue drawn from interviews with people who knew Williams; the story quotes only his line about provision for the sick (also quoted by the International Museum of Surgical Science) and the phrase 'most rigid', both attributed, and does not reproduce other dialogue. Buckler gives first-year figures of 189 patients, while the Provident Foundation gives 189 inpatients for 1897; because of that clash the story uses neither. Williams's later heart operation of 1893 is a separate episode and is left out. The Ptahhotep maxim advises one who has risen from poverty to treat his gains as a trust; the excerpt begins after 'then' and stops before a bracketed editorial insertion.
